summary: Discusses use cases and deployment scenarios for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES), which are services applied to requests or responses at intermediaries. It examines the kinds of things such services could do. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3752 describes ways an Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) processor might inspect or change application messages between a provider and a consumer. It gives examples of services, where processors may be placed, and how people might learn when processing affects content.

questions: open pluggable edge services use cases
what does an opes processor do
subtitle: Examples of services and network arrangements for Open Pluggable Edge Services.

tldr.problem: The OPES architecture allows services to inspect or transform application messages at intermediaries, but designers need examples of services and deployment arrangements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC groups services by whether they act on requests, responses, or create responses. It then describes surrogate and delegate overlays, enterprise use, callout servers, chaining, and failure notification.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC presents use cases and deployment scenarios, not a protocol specification. It refers to separate documents for the OPES architecture and security considerations.

today: RFC 3752 is an Informational RFC published in April 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes use cases and deployment scenarios rather than a protocol.

sections.title: How OPES Processes Messages
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) architecture places application services between a data provider and a data consumer. An OPES processor applies filtering rules to decide when a service runs. The service may run on the processor or on a remote callout server.

This RFC gives examples of services and deployment scenarios. It notes that the IAB had expressed architectural and policy concerns about OPES in RFC 3238.
sections.plainLanguage: An OPES processor can inspect or change application messages as they pass between a provider and a consumer. Rules on the processor determine when a service runs.

sections.title: Services on Requests and Responses
sections.content:
The RFC shows four service points: when a request enters or leaves a processor, and when a response enters or leaves it. A dispatcher checks the rules and invokes services at these points.

Examples of request services include access restrictions, redirection, adding preferences, or monitoring without changing the request. Response services can adapt content or translate it, or can log and monitor it without changing it. A service may also create a response, such as a page assembled with local weather information.
sections.plainLanguage: A processor can act as a request arrives, as it leaves, or while a response passes through. It may change a message, record information about it, or create a response.

sections.title: Surrogate, Delegate, and Enterprise Deployments
sections.content:
OPES entities may operate in an overlay network, a virtual network built over an existing IP network. A surrogate acts for a data provider, while a delegate acts for a data consumer. Their services and administrative domains differ: a surrogate belongs to the provider's domain, and a delegate to the consumer's.

In an enterprise deployment, provider and consumer may share an administrative and trust domain. If an enterprise uses an outside callout server, the RFC says the communication channel should be secure and the server must follow the applicable corporate security policies.
sections.plainLanguage: A surrogate provides services for a content provider; a delegate provides services for a consumer. In a company, one administrative domain may manage both, including any remote service providers it uses.

sections.title: Callout Servers and Chaining
sections.content:
A callout server can share work with an OPES processor or provide a specialized service. The RFC gives virus scanning of large objects as an example of work that may suit a dedicated server.

Processors can be arranged in a series along the content path, so content passes through several processors. Callout servers can also be arranged along the callout path. The RFC notes that chaining callout servers was deferred from version 1 of the protocol discussed there.
sections.plainLanguage: A processor can send work to a separate callout server. Several processors may also handle the same content in sequence.

sections.title: Notifying Users and Providers
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples of how tracing information can help people locate unexpected changes. A provider can inspect trace-related headers in a response, and a consumer can report information showing that a service blocked or changed a request.

Content providers can also use headers to state that a service should not be applied to their content. The RFC notes that a consumer may be able to see services applied by an ISP or enterprise without being able to control them.
sections.plainLanguage: Trace information can help a provider or consumer identify which service changed a message and why. The RFC's examples show how that information can support a report to an administrator.

sections.title: Security Scope
sections.content: This RFC presents use cases and deployment scenarios. For the overall security of OPES entities, it points to the OPES architecture document; it does not add security requirements of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives examples rather than security rules. It points readers to the OPES architecture document for security considerations.
